records.text: Financial Times reporting, as summarized by an unnamed website read by Candace Owens, said Project Aurora began in late 2024 as a pro bono feasibility study for the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation and developed over seven months into consulting contracts reportedly worth $4 million.
records.speaker: Financial Times

appearances.snippet: This website tells us—and I'm going to read this website directly—it says, launched in late 2024, Project Aurora was originally framed as a pro bono feasibility study for the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, a Geneva-registered NGO created with backing from U.S. and Israeli security-linked interests. Over seven months, the project evolved into fully billed ... consulting contracts reportedly worth $4 million. According to a series of leaked documents obtained by the Financial Times, the core of the work focused on estimating the financial costs of various scenarios for Gaza’s post-conflict future.

verification.notes: Financial Times reporting describes seven months of Project Aurora work, beginning as a pro bono feasibility study in October 2024 and developing into contracts worth more than $4 million. BCG’s parliamentary response confirms the pro bono start and later for-fee engagement, while stating that BCG ultimately collected no fees.

records.text: Financial Times reporting, as summarized by an unnamed website read by Candace Owens, described one Project Aurora model offering $9,000 per person to relocate about 500,000 Palestinians and another offering $5,000 plus four years of subsidized housing and one year of food assistance.
records.speaker: Financial Times

appearances.snippet: Two primary models emerged. One proposed a voluntary departure plan. $9,000 in cash per person aimed at relocating around 500,000 Palestinians outside of the Gaza Strip. A second model lowered direct payments to $5,000 but added four years of subsidized housing and one year of food assistance.

verification.notes: The reporting describes one relocation package worth about $9,000 per person for more than 500,000 people. The $5,000 cash payment plus subsidized housing and food were components of that package, not a separate second model as the statement says.

sources.title: BCG modelled plan to relocate Palestinians from Gaza
sources.relevance: Reports one $9,000-per-person relocation package, not two distinct models.

sources.title: The plan to relocate Palestinians from Gaza
sources.relevance: Breaks the $9,000 package into $5,000 cash plus housing and food support, refuting the two-model description.

records.text: Financial Times reporting, as summarized by an unnamed website read by Candace Owens, said BCG leadership directed Project Aurora to stop in April 2025, two senior partners continued it through May, and BCG dismissed the partners and launched an external audit in July.
records.speaker: Financial Times

appearances.snippet: It tells us that by April of 2025, BCG's senior leadership claimed that they had issued some internal guidance to halt the project because concerns began to mount internally about the nature of the client, that being Israel, the implications of the work and the potential reputational damage. ... But the firm would then say that two senior partners continued the project in defiance of their directives, maintaining an unofficial team and billing through alternative structures. ... The project continued through May of 2025 when the Financial Times story broke. In July, BCG quickly dismissed the two partners and launched an external audit.

verification.notes: BCG’s formal response and contemporaneous reporting say the work continued until late May 2025 and that the responsible partners exited within days after an investigation began then. They do not support an April stop followed by a July dismissal and audit; the stated chronology is materially wrong.

sources.relevance: BCG’s formal chronology says work stopped in late May and the partners exited within days.
